articles.title_orig: Milei renews Argentina’s Falklands claim at the UN, urging a ‘peaceful solution’
articles.title_zh: Milei renews Argentina’s Falklands claim at the UN, urging a ‘peaceful solution’
articles.content_orig:
Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas.
“An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Malvinas Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory.
The president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”.
The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”.
“Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.”
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project.
The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company.
The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders.
“For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.
“That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.”
A referendum on the political status of the archipelago was held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said.
Last month, Donald Trump said he was reviewing the US’s neutral position on the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in a first meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham.
“The clear position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just wanted the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British position, and he very much understood what I was saying.”

Why Simon Cowell missed the 'AGT' live shows
"AGT" kicked off Season 21 back in June, with judge Simon Cowell welcoming USA TODAY into his home to discuss the season ahead.
"This year, more than ever, I wanted to see things we'd never seen before, and better," he said of finding new talent each year. "We say, 'What are you going to do?' And they go, 'Trust me, you've never seen this before.' And that's always a great way to start. Because I can't bear seeing worse versions of what we've already seen. That's, for me, a waste of time."
After weeks of thrilling auditions and a brand new Judges' Callback round, the live shows kicked off in late August, which saw magic group Hundred Fingers, singer Lai Noelle, singer/musician Nene Royal and robot act Unitree all earn Golden Buzzers for their performances. The coveted button sent them straight to this week's finale.

As he recovered at home, several stars filled his seat at the judges' table including "Saturday Night Live" star Kenan Thompson, model/former "AGT" judge Heidi Klum and YouTuber KSI.
"He's having an operation that cannot be postponed," host Terry Crews explained during the Aug. 25 episode after pointing out that Cowell's seat at the judge's table was empty. "It's not an emergency, but it can't be put off. Simon, we are sending you our very best wishes for a speedy recovery, and we're looking forward to seeing you back at the judges desk very soon."
Along with Crews, judges Mel B, Howie Mandel and Sofía Vergara held down "AGT" for the remainder of the live shows and semifinals as mesmerizing magicians, thrilling dog acts, impressive singers and more performers took the stage. But in the end, only one winner could take home the prize.

articles.title_orig: Justin Herbert disputes perception of lack of vocal leadership
articles.title_zh: Justin Herbert disputes perception of lack of vocal leadership
articles.content_orig:
Something has kept Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert from fulfilling a skillset that has had coach Jim Harbaugh proclaim that Herbert will be regarded as the best to ever play the game. The disconnect between talent and production has become more pronounced in the early days of the 2026 season, given that the Chargers have lost a pair of home games to two of the worst teams in the league in 2025.
On Wednesday, Herbert’s midweek press conference included questions about a potential increase in vocal leadership.
In response to the first — regarding the possible need for vocal leadership in advance of the Week 3 game at Buffalo — Herbert bristled .
“I think that would imply that there’s no need for vocal leadership before this week,” Herbert said, via Kris Rhim of ESPN. “I think every week is a super important week for us and it’s a great opportunity for us to go play football again and correct the things that we made mistakes on last week and keep pushing forward.”
Herbert interrupted the second question on the subject.
“I don’t think there’s a lack of vocal leadership at all,” Herbert said. “So, I’m going to stop you right there and say that it’s very present. I don’t think anyone is panicked or worried because that’s not going to be the sentiment. It’s moving on to the next play and understand that we’re close, we’ve made mistakes, how do we fix it?”
Herbert reiterated his expectation that there will be no panic, as the team stares at the possibility that 0-2 will become 0-3 and, based on the upcoming schedule (at Seahawks, Broncos, at Chiefs), possibly 0-6 at the bye.
Regardless, something is missing. And it it’s not an issue of Herbert’s talent, it’s something else. Perhaps the players around him aren’t good enough. Perhaps he’s not doing enough to get more out of them. Perhaps the odd-couple pairing of Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is a work in progress that has yet to make enough progress.
A win will change everything. But the team looked flat and overmatched in two straight games the Chargers should have won. Now comes the gauntlet, and there’s a chance the hole will get deeper and deeper with each passing week.

American defense officials are investigating how components from the nation's most advanced stealth aircraft arrived in Hong Kong, after media reports said China obtained F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office acknowledged in a statement that it and the Defense Department are dealing with "a shipment issue" involving parts for the jet.
"We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence," the office stated.
Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles confirmed that the jet components had landed in Hong Kong, though he denied that the missing items were "sensitive equipment." Australia is among several nations whose militaries operate the stealth aircraft.
"Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this," Marles said.
He added: "My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred."
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, as Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. Requests for comment were also submitted to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after a delivery originating in Australia and bound for the United States for repair or disposal months ago was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong. It remains unclear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that the situation prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could gain access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has maintained firm control over Hong Kong since it returned the territory from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas roughly 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been built and 19 countries have placed orders for the aircraft, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China may already have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, regarding the planes. The Defense Science Board, an advisory body to the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is "widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet," according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are continuously updated and improved, counteracting any potential secrets compromised years ago.
Categorized as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings, advanced radar, and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service. Bowman said the plane features advanced sensors to better detect adversaries as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.

Chinese archaeologists find 2,200-year-old ancestor of Dragon Boat Festival treat
When we eat zongzi or other leaf-wrapped food, we can clearly appreciate that this tradition existed since ancient times, says researcher
When the weather turns warm around June, people all across China gather for the annual Dragon Boat Festival, and one of the most famous dishes from the celebration is the zongzi.
Zongzi is a rice dumpling with a delicious filling, wrapped in bamboo leaves before being cooked. The leaves add aroma and flavour to the rice.
In mid-August, a group of scientists from China announced they had discovered an ancient ancestor of zongzi made around 2,200 years ago.
However, Yong Ge, a study author from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Paleoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said it would be a stretch to “directly recognise” the food as zongzi, adding that the comparison is fair but “should not be overinterpreted.”

articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent 2 North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent 2 North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
“Recently, we ⁠sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” said Zelenskyy in his speech on Wednesday.
“These guys are not easy to capture alive,” Zelenskyy said. “One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die.”
He strongly criticised Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, questioning why North Korean soldiers were giving their lives in a war against Ukraine.
“Kim Jong Un uses them like currency and gets something in return,” Zelenskyy said, adding that “countries across Asia have likely already noticed North Korea’s enhanced ballistic missiles and significantly advanced drone capabilities”.
Ukrainian and South Korean estimates indicate North Korea has deployed approximately 15,000 soldiers to support Russia’s war effort since 2024, primarily in the Kursk border region .
Zelenskyy provided no further details regarding the transfer.
Ukrainian forces captured the two North Korean soldiers in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025, in the first known apprehension of Pyongyang’s troops since their deployment to the conflict in 2024. Zelenskyy had previously stated he would consider returning the soldiers to North Korean leader Kim in exchange for Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not deny Zelenskyy’s remarks, but it also declined to confirm operational details of the transfer, citing individual safety and family protection.
The issue was a key topic during a July summit in Ankara, Turkiye, where President Lee Jae Myung met Zelenskyy.
Senior presidential spokesperson Kang Yoo-jung stated afterwards that both leaders agreed to resolve the status of North Korean POWs in Ukraine in accordance with international law and humanitarian principles, while respecting the free will of those involved. This built on a prior agreement reached during the South Korea-Ukraine foreign ministers’ meeting in March, where both nations pledged to cooperate on the POW issue under the same humanitarian framework.

articles.title_orig: How a ban of diesel exports could lead to higher prices — even in the U.S.
articles.title_zh: How a ban of diesel exports could lead to higher prices — even in the U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Diesel prices just hit a new record. Would a U.S. export ban bring relief?
Some Republican lawmakers are calling for a ban on U.S. diesel exports as a way to lower record-high prices. But energy experts warn the move could backfire and drive diesel prices even higher by worsening the global supply crunch.
Average diesel costs hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Tuesday, up 77% from a year ago, according to AAA data. Diesel is vital across the nation's agriculture, trucking and construction sectors, with the price surge especially painful for farmers and small businesses.
Many of the calls for a diesel export ban are coming from lawmakers in states with agriculture-rich economies. Iowa Republicans Sen. Chuck Grassley and Rep. Ashley Hinson are among those calling for American energy companies to be barred from selling diesel outside of the U.S., arguing that could help lower prices for Americans.
Tennessee Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican, introduced two related bills on Sept. 17, one that would ban diesel exports through January 2027 and another that would trigger an export ban any time diesel hit a national average of $5 or more per gallon.
"W diesel $6.57 in Iowa why doesn't Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag products bc food prices were inflated. High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME," Grassley wrote in a Sept. 19 social media post.
President Trump on Tuesday said his administration is considering a diesel export ban as a way to lower costs for businesses and farmers, according to the New York Times.
"I've called for it," Mr. Trump said of a diesel export ban, the newspaper reported. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
Mr. Trump and Energy Secretary Chris Wright have discussed a diesel export ban, although no final decisions have been made, according to administration officials.
Why a diesel export ban wouldn't ease prices
But experts say a proposed diesel export ban wouldn't ease prices because it misdiagnoses the problem. They note that the U.S. exports diesel because domestic refineries produce more of the fuel than the country consumes. But because diesel is traded on global markets, prices have surged due to production and shipping disruptions caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine-Russia war.
In July, Russia banned exports of diesel amid Ukraine's attacks on the country's production facilities, removing supply from an already tight international market. Russia typically produces about one in nine barrels of diesel worldwide, which means it is now effectively supplying none to the market, Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at GasBuddy, told CBS News.
Meanwhile, barring U.S. refiners from selling diesel overseas could increase the global shortage, pushing diesel prices higher, he added.
An export ban "is very likely to backfire," De Haan said. "Most lawmakers think, 'Oh, hey, this sounds easy, let's just back up products in the United States,' but that doesn't put them in the place they need to be. It's just fraught with problems that haven't been thought out."
U.S. refineries produce about 5.3 million barrels of so-called distillates — the energy industry's term for fuels that include diesel, home heating oil and jet fuel — per day, while domestic demand absorbs about 3.6 million barrels per day for these products, according to De Haan.
Diesel prices have soared because of global shortages, even though U.S. production exceeds domestic demand. Because diesel trades internationally, American consumers and businesses pay prices shaped by those global dynamics, he explains.
A diesel export ban could also lead to unintended consequences for U.S. production, experts told CBS News. American refiners could respond by cutting output, putting more upward pressure on diesel prices, or even shifting to producing other types of fuel that they could legally sell outside the U.S.
"Refineries are just going to try and get around it — they have a business to run," De Haan said. "There will be shifts that happen whether refineries start producing something that's not quite fully refined and exporting that, or they could very easily switch over to more jet fuel production."
Domestic refineries would likely cut diesel production in response to an export ban, removing domestic supplies that the ban was supposed to protect, Tracy Shuchart, CEO of energy consulting firm Hilltower Resource Advisors, said in a Sept. 15 social media post.
Foreign buyers would likely cement new deals with non-U.S. diesel suppliers, potentially weakening domestic companies in the long term, she added.
So what could lower diesel prices?
Instead of an export ban, the U.S. could turn to other measures to ease diesel prices. De Haan said the Trump administration could extend an existing waiver of a law, the Jones Act, that requires goods shipped among U.S. ports to be carried on U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed vessels. That waiver is set to expire on Nov. 15.
Another option would be to temporarily waive a federal rule that requires refiners and retailers to sell a certain amount of renewable fuel, mostly ethanol, a step De Haan said could lower fuel prices by about 10 cents to 20 cents a gallon.
"Aside from that, the only thing that the administration really can do is get the Strait reopened," he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, the vital Middle East waterway that, before the conflict with Iran, carried a fifth of global oil supply.
Separately, De Haan said that fears about diesel shortages in the U.S. are unfounded. Although a handful of gas stations may report being out of fuel at any given time, data from GasBuddy, a real-time tracking service, shows no diesel shortages.
"It's not abnormal for stations to run out of gasoline —premium, mid-grade, diesel — and there can be a lot of different reasons for that," he told CBS News. "On a daily basis, there's probably somewhere in the ballpark of 0.5% to 1% of stations that may temporarily run out."
Some stations may also opt to delay buying a new shipment of diesel, given the current high prices, hoping to see lower costs down the road, he added.

articles.title_orig: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.title_zh: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.content_orig:
An Iowa judge has dismissed President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling company, the Des Moines Register and Gannett.
In a written ruling on Wednesday, Judge Scott Beattie of Iowa’s Fifth Judicial District threw out the lawsuit by Trump, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa State Senator Brad Zaun.
The suit was dismissed with prejudice, which means Trump cannot file the same claim again. A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president plans to appeal to the Iowa Supreme Court, vowing to pursue “a just and winning conclusion.”
The ruling marks a setback in Trump’s broader legal campaign against news outlets, including ongoing lawsuits against the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.
The lawsuit centered on a 2024 poll published days before the presidential election that showed Vice President Kamala Harris with a lead in Iowa that did not pan out in the actual election results. The suit alleged that the poll and the reporting around it aimed to artificially give Democrats an edge in the last week of the campaign.
Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun accused the defendants of knowingly publishing false polling information and, even if unintentional, negligently publishing false information.
Regarding the claim that the poll violated the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, Beattie wrote that the “Iowa Poll and its reporting are fully protected political speech,” noting that plaintiffs’ lawsuit “does not allege the elements that would place that speech within the fraud exception.”
But Beattie noted that even if the First Amendment issues were set aside, the claims still didn’t meet Iowa law’s basic requirements. While Trump, Miller-Meeks, and Zaun tried to use the state’s consumer fraud statute, Beattie wrote that it applies only to consumer transactions.
Regarding the alleged fraudulent misrepresentation, Beattie writes that there was “no representation made to induce any plaintiff to act and no act taken in reliance on the truth of the polls.”
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the nonprofit free speech group that took up Selzer’s defense, said in a statement, “We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought.”
“The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’ That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law,” FIRE chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said.
The First Amendment victory in Iowa came on the same day that a federal judge in Washington heard arguments in CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s lawsuit over Trump’s White House media ban. The judge in that case said he would rule soon.
Des Moines Register owner Gannett, which renamed itself USA Today Co. last year, also celebrated the victory on Wednesday.
“This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action,” said Polly Grunfeld Sack, the media company’s chief legal counsel.

Major tech, AI execs to dine with Trump, Xipublished at 03:06 BST
Kali Hays US technology reporter
Elon Musk was among a delegation of tech executives that joined Trump in Beijing last May
As the US and China race to develop more capable AI, discussion of the technology is set to be on the menu on Thursday.
Some of the most notable names in tech, including Satya Nadella of Microsoft, Tim Cook of Apple, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Jensen Huang of Nvidia, are expected to be dining with President Trump and Xi Jinping.
Also set to attend are Jeff Bezos, chairman of Amazon, Elon Musk, boss of Tesla and SpaceX, Sundar Pichai, boss of Google, Michael Dell, of Dell computers, and Jane Fraser, boss of Citi bank, representatives of the White House said.
When Trump travelled to China in May for a meeting with Xi, he also brought along Musk, Huang and Cook, along with a dozen other tech and business executives. At the time, public fears around AI tools getting outside of human control were not as widespread as they are now.
Altman and Huang, both huge beneficiaries of the recent AI boom, have recently been vocal in their ideas of how the US should deal with the prospect of future AI tools going outside human control.
Huang, like Trump, favours a more hands-off approach by the government. Altman has also supported the idea of AI companies being left responsible for safety of their tools, but on Monday urged the US to take a leadership position on global discussions of AI policy.

Xi is accompanied on this trip by some of the most senior figures in his government, according to Chinese state-run news outlet Xinhua.
Arriving on the same plane as the Chinese leader were Cai Qi, a member of the Chinese Communist Party's Politburo Standing Committee who's widely known as Xi's right-hand man, as well as foreign minister Wang Yi.
There are also officials who had arrived in the US earlier, including Vice Premier He Lifeng, who met US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in New York ahead of the summit, and Xie Feng, China's Ambassador to the US.

Why Xi might not want Chinese business leaders on this trippublished at 01:46 BST

As we reported earlier, it's unclear which business executives, if any, are coming on this trip with Xi.
It would be a stark contrast if several American AI CEOs attended a state dinner at which no Chinese AI CEOs appeared to be present - especially since Trump took CEOs with him to Beijing in May.
But Xi's decision is not surprising. He may see it as a risk for Beijing.
He will have seen how events like this can become a media scrum - and the last thing the Chinese leader wants is a CEO contradicting his message at any point.

The agreement, which took effect last year and was due to expire in November, will now run until at least 10 January.
It came after lengthy talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York at the weekend, and then in Washington on Wednesday.
The fact that it took so long to effectively kick the can down the road indicates just how tricky negotiations between the world's two biggest economies are proving to be.

But a slew of counter measures from China, including restrictions on crucial rare earths exports, dealt a stunning blow that left the two countries in a stalemate.
The question now is can any real progress be made when the two leaders sit down to talks on Thursday.
